arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE PAPER, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The corpus first prints this person at the Democrat of 4 June 1834, column 9, so they are in the town's paper by 1834-06-04 and at no stated time before it; nothing reached says when they came. Last printed 1834-06-04.

lives_at.note: Not attested. NOTHING IS BEING WITHHELD HERE: no source reached says where this person lived, and 52 households in this dataset were already in that position before this one was written.

works_at.note: Not attested as a structure this project models. The trade is documented; the premises are not one of the committed records.

present_on_scene_date.note: THE CORPUS STOPS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Last printed 1834-06-04, at the Democrat of 4 June 1834, column 9, and nothing reached either follows this person to 1 July 1835 or says they left. A documented resident whose whereabouts on one day are unknown is `uncertain` here rather than dropped: that is the same distinction index.json draws for Jeremiah Porter, and it is a finding rather than a gap.

persons.name: E. L. Thrall

occupation.note: THE TRADE IS THE PAPER'S. The corpus reads it as clothier, tailor, at the Democrat of 4 June 1834, column 9. The residents vocabulary's nearest period-correct word for it is `clothier`, and where the corpus prints more than one trade they are all named here rather than reduced to the one the vocabulary could take.

persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'E. L. TRRALL' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 4 June 1834, column 9. The corpus associates the name with South Water Street; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `clothier` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Edward L. Thrall,” (f1839_v0056, printed page 41, ward 1, voting for William B. Ogden). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Thrall' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins E. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

resident_research.evidence_for: No reliable record found in the reviewed web, institutional-history, digitized-book, newspaper-index and genealogy-finding-aid searches could be tied to this 1835 Chicago person without relying on the name alone.
resident_research.notes: No candidate fact is asserted unless a source bridges the candidate to the 1835 Chicago record by more than name similarity.
resident_research.summary: The 1837 election return prints 'Edward L. Thrall' — the forename expanding the E. and the middle initial agreeing — which carries that he was in Chicago and in ward 1 on 2 May 1837. It is a different record from the 1839 listing already on his card, though printed in the same volume. The papers give the trade: clothier, 4 June 1834.

merge_ruling.for_merge: E. L. Thrall is a documented tradesman of the town — the Democrat of 4 June 1834, column 9, gives him the trade (clothier, tailor) at Charles Taylor's old stand on South Water Street, the business handed to him by its previous owner; Fergus 1843 prints 'Thrall, E. L., clerk, Charles Walker & Co.' and Norris 1844 'Thrall, E. L. clerk, at C. Walker & Co.' The only entry of the stem on any of the town's own rolls is 'Trall, E.L.' on the poll list of 1835 (line 367), and a documented tradesman keeping a South Water Street stand is a man who could be expected on it. The town holds exactly one bearer of each spelling, both 'E. L.'
merge_ruling.against_merge: THE TWO BODIES OF EVIDENCE NEVER TOUCH. Searched over every deposited text and every extracted claim: 'Trall' occurs in exactly two places, the 1835 poll list and genealogytrails' transcription of it — and the Chicago Democrat, Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843, Norris 1844, the Newberry locality cards and Moses & Kirkland set only Thrall, never Trall. The rolls know one spelling, the press and the books know the other, and no publication is caught setting both. That is the Pruyne shape exactly, and it is refused for the same reason. A reader may note the paper's own printing of the trade advertisement reads 'E. L. TRRALL' — a garble that is neither spelling cleanly, and could be read toward either — but a single garbled printing is not a title caught SETTING BOTH, which is what C9 requires, and reading it toward the fold is the reader's willingness, not the printer's inconsistency. D7, and the cards stay two. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT IS NOT A PAGE BUT A COUNT, in C12's shape moved from the forename to the surname — the closed roll leaves the documented man exactly one entry he can be, and the exhaustion is worked over the whole roll and printed rather than asserted. C12 as written reaches a FORENAME only, so firing it on a surname is itself a rule to write. T-1135 owns that question for Pruyne/Pryne and the rule it writes is the one this pair waits on.

roles.note: THE BOUND IS THE SOURCE'S, NOT THE MAN'S. This role is carried by the card's 1835 occupation block and is dated by what the cited source or sources are ABOUT, which is why `precision` can be no better than the span they cover. The span reaches 1835, so this role stands in the scene-date view. The printing the trade was read off is not on the card and is fetched by T-1254.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name E. L. Thrall as a clothier at Chicago 1 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. thrall_e_l, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 — f1843_e2442 (a single entry); thrall_e_l, Norris's Chicago directory of 1844 — n1844_e1771 (a single entry).
